newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico opposition voted against petrochemical law.
newsitem.headline: Mexico opposition voted against petrochemical law.

text.p: Mexico's conservative opposition National Action Party (PAN) voted against the government's plans to privatise the petrochemical industry when they were debated in the Senate Tuesday, party officials said Wednesday.

The bill passed thanks to the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party's (PRI) large majority, but all the PAN senators joined their left-wing PRD colleagues and one PRI dissident in voting against it.

A PAN Senate official said that her party's senators had objected to the government's proposal to allow foreigners to take 100 percent ownership of new secondary petrochemical industry projects, saying they should be limited to minority stakes.

The government earlier this month presented a proposal allowing foreign investors to take 100 pct of new secondary petrochemical plants and 49 percent of existing plant. A previous plan allowing foreigners 100 pct of existing plant was scrapped after fierce opposition from within the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party.

PAN Senator Rosendo Villareal, who represents the northern state of Coahuila, had days earlier presented an amendment -- later defeated -- to limit foreign investment to 49 percent of new secondary petrochemical plants.

"Villareal said that control of the secondary petrochemical industry must stay in Mexican hands, so that it is managed and developed with a patriotic and authentically nationalist sense", the PAN said in a statement.
The party did say, however, that it supported the idea of injecting some private capital into the petrochemical industry to help it modernise.

Business leaders have expressed growing concern of late that the PAN, which originally billed itself as a free-market, pro-business party, is becoming increasingly erratic on economic policy as key 1997 elections draw near.
The party voted against Mexico's private pensions reform in Congress earlier this year, for example, even though it had previously assured business leaders it supported the plan.
